crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Research credits from engineering records covers the practice of reconstructing a claim for research and development tax relief out of the artefacts a software or AI team already produces. The records in question are commit histories, issue trackers, design documents, experiment logs, model training runs and the correspondence around them. The work sits inside tax and jurisdictional compliance because the same engineering evidence must be mapped onto different national definitions of qualifying research, and the claim is only as strong as the trail that supports it.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The raw material lives in version control systems such as Git, in ticket and wiki platforms, and in experiment tracking and cloud compute billing. Practitioners pull these sources into a data warehouse or a document store, then link each technical activity to a time period, a person and a cost centre. Compute spend, contractor invoices and payroll feed the same pipeline, because a credit claim is a financial calculation built on technical evidence. Access controls matter here, since the records often contain unreleased product detail.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The usual approach is to define the qualifying questions first, then search the engineering record for evidence that answers them. Staff interviews fill the gaps that logs cannot explain, particularly the uncertainty that existed at the start of a project and the alternatives that were tried and abandoned. Each candidate project is scored against the local test, whether that is technological uncertainty, a systematic process or an advance in the field. The output is a schedule that ties narrative, technical evidence and cost together, and it is normally reviewed by someone who did not write it.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risks are overclaiming, weak contemporaneous evidence and inconsistent treatment across jurisdictions where the same work is judged by different rules. Records must be retained for the statutory period, and personal data inside tickets and chat logs needs a lawful basis and redaction before it reaches an adviser or an auditor. Provenance is the whole argument: a claim should be traceable from the figure in the return back to the commit, the ticket or the invoice that supports it. Where a credit is later challenged, the file is the defence, and reconstructed narratives written years afterwards are the weakest part of it.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect more automation in the evidence gathering, with tooling that reads repositories and cloud bills directly rather than relying on annual questionnaires. Regulators in several countries have been tightening documentation standards and asking for more granular technical detail, which pushes teams toward keeping the record clean as work happens rather than rebuilding it at year end. The open question is how generative and machine learning work is treated, since iterative experimentation fits some definitions of research well and others poorly. The site tracks 229 compliance and regulation pages, and this area will keep moving as those rules are tested.
